entries.seminar_title: Do Climate Shocks Redirect Science? Evidence from Coral Bleaching
entries.speaker: Sahila Kudalkar
entries.abstract: What shifts the direction of scientific research? Reallocating scientific effort is costly and slow, yet researchers must adapt to persistent climate shocks to keep pace with a changing natural world. This study examines how global coral bleaching events reallocate scientific effort, comparing publication volume and composition for bleached versus unbleached coral species. I then test whether this shift in academic attention translates into economically valuable outputs: new compounds and fluorescent protein patents. Bleached species see a rise in publications, driven not only by bleaching research itself but also by increased attention to their biochemical properties and fluorescent proteins. This attention shift is matched by a rise in fluorescent-protein patent applications and grants, but not by any change in compound discovery. The publication response is significant after the first global bleaching event but fades in subsequent ones — consistent with a shifting baseline, as bleaching becomes routine post-2010. Together, the results offer preliminary evidence that basic science and firm innovation both respond to the initial shock of a climate event, but that the response weakens as the shock becomes recurrent.

entries.seminar_title: What would it cost to end extreme poverty?
entries.speaker: Roshni Sahoo
entries.abstract: We study poverty minimization via direct transfers, framing this as a statistical learning problem while retaining the information constraints faced by real-world programs. Using nationally representative household consumption surveys from 34 countries that together account for 76% of the world’s poor, we estimate that reducing the poverty rate to 1% (from a baseline of 13%) would cost $211B nominal per year. This is 4.0 times the corresponding reduction in the aggregate poverty gap, but only 19% of the cost of universal basic income. Extrapolated globally, the results imply a cost of 0.28% of global GDP to (approximately) end extreme poverty.

entries.seminar_title: Public-Sector Pay, Worker Selection, and Government Performance: Evidence from Locality Pay Areas in the U.S.
entries.speaker: Diego Tocre
entries.abstract: How does geographically differentiated public-sector pay affect the composition and performance of the federal workforce? We study the creation and expansion of Locality Pay Areas (LPAs), geographic zones where federal salaries are raised to keep pace with local private-sector wages across U.S. labor markets. Leveraging staggered county-level variation in LPA adoption and administrative payroll data, we find that federal employment in the average treated county rises 14% within seven years, an implied labor-supply elasticity near two. Growth is concentrated in occupations with strong private-sector outside options, and comes from relocating incumbent federal workers out of the urban core rather than new hires. We find no effect on service contracting.
